explanations.answer: Put your house in order because you will die
explanations.explanation: Isaiah, the prophet, comes to Hezekiah, king of Judah, and says, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.’” That is a heavy message, and I think it lands hard. This part of the story is just heavy, so I'll let it sit.

explanations.answer: Rest a while and you will feel better soon
explanations.explanation: I wish that were the message, friend, but Isaiah isn't carrying a nice little note saying to take it easy. The LORD says, “Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.” This is a heavy moment for Hezekiah, king of Judah. Hold on to it, though, because the story keeps moving.

explanations.answer: Send for a doctor from Egypt right away
explanations.explanation: No doctor shows up anywhere in this scene, baker. Isaiah, the prophet, brings a message from the LORD: “Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.” Hezekiah, king of Judah, hears it straight. It's a heavy moment, and I think it hits him hard.

explanations.answer: prays
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Hezekiah, king of Judah, turns his face to the wall and prays to the LORD. No crowd, no speech, just him talking to God. When the news is this heavy, I think there's no better place to take it.

explanations.answer: sings
explanations.explanation: Hezekiah, king of Judah, isn't singing, baker. The text says he turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD. Trust me, nobody wants to hear my singing in a moment like this either. A prayer was what he brought.

explanations.answer: shouts
explanations.explanation: No shouting in this one, friend. Hezekiah, king of Judah, turns his face to the wall and prays to the LORD. It's a prayer, plain and simple. I'm the loud one in this bakery, and even I can see this moment calls for a prayer.

explanations.answer: How he walked before Him faithfully
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Hezekiah prays, “Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion; I have done what is good in Your sight.” He's honest and plain with the LORD, with nothing fancy added. I'd want to pray the same way when I'm worn down to my last crumb.

explanations.answer: The temple he built for His name
explanations.explanation: Hezekiah doesn't mention a temple in this prayer, friend. What he says is, “Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion; I have done what is good in Your sight.” His words are about how he walked before the LORD. Keep that line close, because it's the heart of his prayer.

explanations.answer: The armies he raised for Judah
explanations.explanation: No armies in this prayer, baker. Hezekiah asks the LORD to remember “how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion.” He also says, “I have done what is good in Your sight.” It's all about his walk with the LORD, and not one word about soldiers.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says, friend. After his prayer, it says, “And Hezekiah wept bitterly.” Those are real tears, and they're a big deal in this story. I think this man is hurting.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The text says plainly, “And Hezekiah wept bitterly.” There's no staying calm here, only tears. The LORD notices them too, as we'll see in a moment.

explanations.answer: Go back and tell Hezekiah His message
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The word of the LORD comes to Isaiah and says, “Go back and tell Hezekiah the leader of My people…” Isaiah turns right around, like a guy halfway to the car who remembers he left his keys. The difference is that this time he's going back for the best news ever.

explanations.answer: Keep walking and leave the palace
explanations.explanation: Isaiah doesn't keep walking, friend. The LORD says, “Go back and tell Hezekiah the leader of My people…” So Isaiah turns around instead of heading out. There's still more to say to the king.

explanations.answer: Send a servant with a sealed letter
explanations.explanation: No letter and no servant in this scene, baker. The LORD tells Isaiah himself, “Go back and tell Hezekiah the leader of My people…” Isaiah is the one who delivers the message. I like it that way, because it's more personal.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The LORD says, “I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. I will surely heal you.” Sit with that one for a second. Hezekiah went from “you will not recover” to “I will surely heal you,” and I'd say that's quite a turn.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: It's actually true, baker. The LORD tells Hezekiah, “I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. I will surely heal you.” It's a complete turn from the first message. I think Hezekiah's tears just got a very good answer.

explanations.answer: The house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The LORD says that on the third day from now, Hezekiah will go up to the house of the LORD. Three days ago he was told to put his house in order, and now he's getting a date for church. That's quite a turnaround.

explanations.answer: The top of the city wall
explanations.explanation: Not the wall, baker. The LORD says Hezekiah will go up to the house of the LORD on the third day from now. A sick man heading up to worship in three days is a big promise. The LORD is the one making it.

explanations.answer: The roof of the palace
explanations.explanation: The roof isn't in this promise, friend. The LORD says that on the third day from now, Hezekiah will go up to the house of the LORD. I think that's a better view anyway. It's the place where he can thank God in person.

explanations.answer: fifteen
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says, “I will add fifteen years to your life.” Fifteen whole years added to a man who was told to put his house in order. I've baked batches that didn't come out that generous.

explanations.answer: twenty
explanations.explanation: Close, but it isn't twenty, friend. The LORD says, “I will add fifteen years to your life.” It's fifteen exactly. That's still a lot of extra time for Hezekiah.

explanations.answer: five
explanations.explanation: Five is too low, baker. The LORD says, “I will add fifteen years to your life.” Fifteen is three times that. The LORD gives Hezekiah a lot more time than you picked.

explanations.answer: David
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The LORD says He will defend the city “for My sake and for the sake of My servant David.” He's called David there, and earlier He's called “the God of your father David” in the same message. The LORD says His own sake comes first, and David comes right after.

explanations.answer: Moses
explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is a great name, but he's not the one here. The LORD says, “for My sake and for the sake of My servant David.” Earlier in the message He also calls Himself “the God of your father David.” David's name is the one in the promise.

explanations.answer: Solomon
explanations.explanation: Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (1 Kings 2:12), isn't the name here, baker. The LORD says He will defend the city “for My sake and for the sake of My servant David.” He also calls Himself “the God of your father David” in that message. So David is the answer.

explanations.answer: A poultice of figs
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Isaiah says, “Prepare a poultice of figs.” They bring it, apply it to the boil, and Hezekiah recovers. One ingredient, and the recipe card is done. I wish all my recipes were that short.

explanations.answer: A bowl of salt water
explanations.explanation: Salt water isn't in this recipe, friend. Isaiah says, “Prepare a poultice of figs.” They apply it to the boil, and Hezekiah recovers. Figs are the only thing on the list.

explanations.answer: A wrap of myrrh and linen
explanations.explanation: No myrrh or linen here, baker. Isaiah says, “Prepare a poultice of figs.” They put it on the boil, and Hezekiah recovers. It's a short list with just figs on it.

explanations.answer: A sign that the LORD would heal him
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Hezekiah asked Isaiah, “What will be the sign that the LORD will heal me and that I will go up to the house of the LORD on the third day?” He wanted a sign about the healing itself. Isaiah then answers him with a choice.

explanations.answer: A prayer for the people of the city
explanations.explanation: This question isn't about a prayer for the city, baker. Hezekiah asked Isaiah, “What will be the sign that the LORD will heal me and that I will go up to the house of the LORD on the third day?” It's a request for a sign of his own healing. Isaiah takes it up from there.

explanations.answer: A blessing over the sons of the king
explanations.explanation: No blessing on any sons in this question, friend. Hezekiah asked Isaiah, “What will be the sign that the LORD will heal me and that I will go up to the house of the LORD on the third day?” It's a sign of healing he asked for. Isaiah gives him one.

explanations.answer: A shadow goes forward or back ten steps
explanations.explanation: That's the choice, baker. Isaiah asks, “Would you like the shadow to go forward ten steps, or back ten steps?” It's a sign from the LORD that He will do what He has promised. Forward or back, Hezekiah gets to pick.

explanations.answer: The sun stands still or sets early
explanations.explanation: The sun isn't part of this offer, friend. Isaiah asks, “Would you like the shadow to go forward ten steps, or back ten steps?” The sign is about a shadow and ten steps. It's a sign from the LORD that He will do what He has promised.

explanations.answer: Rain falls or the river runs dry
explanations.explanation: No rain and no river in this choice, baker. Isaiah asks, “Would you like the shadow to go forward ten steps, or back ten steps?” The sign is about a shadow moving ten steps. It's a sign from the LORD that He will do what He has promised.

explanations.answer: Going forward is easy but going back is not
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Hezekiah answers, “It is easy for the shadow to lengthen ten steps, but not for it to go back ten steps.” He picks the harder one. I'd have taken the easy one and a second cookie, but Hezekiah goes for the bigger sign.

explanations.answer: Going back is quicker for everyone to watch
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different reason, baker. Hezekiah says, “It is easy for the shadow to lengthen ten steps, but not for it to go back ten steps.” Nothing is said about how quick it is. He picks back because it's the harder one.

explanations.answer: Going forward would frighten the whole city
explanations.explanation: Nobody in the text is afraid of the shadow, friend. Hezekiah explains, “It is easy for the shadow to lengthen ten steps, but not for it to go back ten steps.” That's his whole reason. Forward is easy, so he asks for back.

explanations.answer: Ahaz
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Isaiah calls out to the LORD, and He brings the shadow back the ten steps it had descended on the stairway of Ahaz. Ahaz was Hezekiah's father (2 Kings 16:20). The LORD does the very thing Hezekiah said was hard.

explanations.answer: Solomon
explanations.explanation: Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (1 Kings 2:12), isn't on this stairway, friend. The text says the LORD brings the shadow back ten steps on the stairway of Ahaz. Ahaz was Hezekiah's father (2 Kings 16:20). So the stairway belongs to Ahaz.

explanations.answer: Jehoshaphat
explanations.explanation: Jehoshaphat, a king of Judah (1 Kings 22:41), isn't the name on this stairway, baker. The text says the LORD brings the shadow back ten steps on the stairway of Ahaz. Ahaz was Hezekiah's father (2 Kings 16:20). I still say Jehoshaphat is a fun name to say.
